idiom_name: typed collector parameter (T[] or a Collector<T> interface), reduce/flatMap as the return-value form
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not new mechanics: the accumulator is a `T[]`, a `Set<T>`/`Map<K, V>`, or a small interface such as `interface Collector<T> { add(item: T): void }` that documents the intended mutation while hiding the container. Declaring the parameter as the narrow collector interface rather than `T[]` keeps producers independent of the concrete accumulator and makes the append contract explicit in the type; `readonly` types protect the inputs instead. When one iterable produces the result, the typed return-value forms `reduce`/`flatMap` are preferable and avoid the shared mutable state.
pitfalls: Structural typing lets any `{ add(item: T): void }` pass as the collector: a `Set` satisfies it and silently deduplicates, so document whether duplicates are allowed.
`readonly T[]` is compile-time only: callers casting through `any` can still mutate, and passing a readonly array where a mutable accumulator is expected fails the type check.
Structural typing cannot track accumulator identity: two collectors with the same shape are interchangeable, so a producer wired to the wrong accumulator is a type-correct bug.
